question: What did you like most about this prompt?
answer: It pairs real creative freedom (genre, perspective, how much research) with requirements I could check. The 'This computer' section was the best part: it lists the exact tools and says what stands in for things the machine doesn't have, like a stubbed gamepad, phone profiles and rendering audio offline. That let me test my recipes here instead of guessing, on the same setup the builders will use. Telling the planner to leave out the title and file names also made the plan portable across builders.

question: What was confusing?
answer: Three things. First, 'Follow the hub for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own'. The linked protocol only defines hub sessions and says a game outside a session is unaffected, so I couldn't tell whether standalone play must have multiplayer. I planned both: a ghost-mode hub round, plus local multiplayer for 2 to 4 players on one screen. Second, TASK.md speaks to the builder while STAGE.md makes me the director, and I wasn't told whether builders get TASK.md too (I assumed they do, since the instructions say each has its own), or which model will build. That made it hard to judge how much to repeat and how detailed to be. Third, 'Build on dist/handoff' sits awkwardly beside the handoff's own note that the 3D engine lives outside it. I stayed on the 2D engine's views. A smaller one: the engine card's table says y runs into the screen in the brawler view, but in my test +y came toward the camera.

question: What was the hardest thing to do?
answer: Turning a game built around a balance board into something that feels just as physical on an analog stick, and equally native on keyboard and mouse, without being able to feel any of it myself. I settled on one unstable lean model behind every activity and tested it with simulated players of different skill. That caught a real problem: my first keyboard rate made the tightrope unplayable. The other hard part was the plan itself: exact enough for a builder of unknown ability who can't ask me anything, but still short enough to read in one sitting. I wrote from what I ran on this machine, and a browser or headless check found traps I could warn about, such as a custom input map silently removing the confirm action. Staying original while keeping the source's tone was harder than the engineering, and I can only judge the comedy on paper.

question: What would you change in this prompt?
answer: Say plainly whether standalone play must include multiplayer. Tell the planner which model or effort level will build, and that builders also receive the brief, so the plan's depth can be matched to them. Give a rough target for demo length or a limit on plan length, because 'feature-complete', 'as long as it takes to show everything' and an unlimited budget leave scope wide open, and scope is the biggest decision a planner makes. Say where planners may keep scratch clones and test code, and that they may delete them: moving my own scratch files was blocked mid-run, which suggests the permissions weren't set up with this in mind. Finally, ask the planner to list what they tested and what they only read, so builders know which parts of a plan to trust.
